volumes.title: A Milestone, Corrected
volumes.text:
Sketch the first. Pencil. The milestone on the Fell road, three miles out of Emberwick.

My name is Corwen Ashby. For forty years I painted the signs of this town: BUTCHER, FERRY, NO HAWKERS, all of it dead level, and gilded where the money ran to it. I retired on Friday. On Saturday my sister gave me this sketchbook and told me to go and draw something that was not a letter. So I am walking up into the Northern Fells for twelve days, a sketch a day, and I have begun with a milestone because it had lettering on it. I am not proud of that.

The sketch: one stone, which leans. I have drawn it upright. I find I have also corrected the spacing of EMBERWICK, which the mason crowded at the K. The stone does not look like the stone. The lettering is excellent.

volumes.title: The Gate at Stoneladle
volumes.text:
Sketch the second. Pencil. A field gate at Stoneladle Farm, where I lodge at both ends of my twelve days in the Fells.

Mrs. Tolley keeps the farm with her granddaughter Marrin, who is eleven, and a dog called Biscuit, who is everywhere. There is a board at the lane end which once said STONELADLE and now says ST N L DL. Forty years a signwriter, I noticed that before I noticed the mountains.

The sketch: five bars, two posts, one hinge. I ruled the bars against the edge of my pencil tin. Marrin said it was a very good gate, but that theirs sags. She is right. Theirs drops a full hand at the latch end, and a hen was sitting on it. I have drawn the gate the joiner intended. The hen I left out, as she would not hold still.

volumes.title: Sheep, So Called
volumes.text:
Sketch the third. Pencil, much rubbed. Sheep on the rough pasture above Stoneladle Farm.

I am Corwen Ashby, retired signwriter, up in the Northern Fells to learn to draw what I cannot rule. A letter stays where you put it. A sheep does not. I began on a ewe’s head and she turned round. I began on her other end and she walked behind a different sheep. By noon the page held eleven beginnings: an ear, a back, something that might be a knee.

The sketch, as it stands: a cloud with four legs, and near it a smaller cloud. Marrin Tolley, who is eleven and belongs to the farm, studied it gravely and asked which one was the dog. Neither is the dog. I have written SHEEP underneath in a good plain capital, and that at least nobody could mistake.

volumes.title: Rain on Hollin Tarn
volumes.text:
Sketch the fourth. Pencil and weather. Hollin Tarn, two hours above the farm.

The tarn is a small dark water in a cup of the fell, with one holly tree on the far bank that has no business growing so high. I sat on my coat and got the far shore in: a long line, steady, the best of the trip. I was forty years a signwriter and I can still pull a line. Then it rained. It did not rain much. It rained in single fat drops, slowly, as if counting. Each one raised a blister on the paper and floated a little of the pencil off sideways. I held my hat over the book and drew under it like a man reading a private letter.

The sketch: one fine shore, one holly, nineteen pale spots. The spots are more like water than anything I drew.

volumes.title: Marrin’s Method
volumes.text:
Sketch the fifth. Pencil, done fast. Biscuit, the dog at Stoneladle Farm.

Marrin Tolley is eleven and draws on the backs of feed bills. Today she showed me how. You look at the dog, she says, not at the paper, and you do not stop your pencil until the dog is finished or gone. She did Biscuit in about the time it takes to sneeze. It was all one line, with a loop for the tail, and it was him exactly, scratching. I am a signwriter. In forty years I never put down a line I was not looking at. I tried it. My pencil went off the page and across my knee.

The sketch, third attempt: a scribble with one ear. It is wrong in every measurable way. It is also, I am annoyed to say, more like a dog than my sheep were like sheep.

volumes.title: The Kettle, Boiling
volumes.text:
Sketch the sixth. Pencil. My own boots, at the foot of Kettle Crag.

Kettle Crag is the highest of the fells behind Emberwick, and the reason I came this way. I have looked up at it from the town for sixty years and meant to draw its top. The shepherds say the Kettle is always boiling, which is their way of telling you the summit sits in cloud. It sat in cloud today. I waited three hours on a flat rock. In the first hour I was patient. In the second I ate my bread. In the third I drew my boots, because they were there.

The sketch: two boots, laces undone, the left one fallen over. No ruler came near it. It is the first drawing in this book that looks like the thing. I shall try the Crag again on my way back.

volumes.title: Jessop Rudd’s Wall
volumes.text:
Sketch the seventh. Pencil. A drystone wall below Rooksgate, with the man who is mending it.

Jessop Rudd has walled these fells since boyhood, and he let me watch him close a gap. He picks up a stone, turns it once, and it goes where it was always going to go. He does not measure. I said that in my trade, signwriting, we snap a chalk line first. He said in his trade the hill would only laugh. I drew the wall stone by stone, and found I enjoyed it. Stones in a course are like letters in a word: each one different, all sitting on the same line, and the gaps mattering as much as the stones.

The sketch: fourteen feet of wall, and at the end a hat with a man under it. Rudd said the wall was fair. He did not mention the man.

volumes.title: Indoors at Hag Beck
volumes.text:
Sketch the eighth. Pencil, by candle. The inside of the shepherds’ hut at Hag Beck.

It blew hard all day, and Jessop Rudd the waller advised me, a town signwriter with a sketchbook, to stop where there was a roof. So I have spent the eighth of my twelve days in a stone hut the size of a cart, with a hearth, a bench, and a kettle that takes forty minutes to think about boiling. I drew what there was. One candle in a bottle. My socks on a string over the fire, steaming. The kettle. The door, bulging when the wind leaned on it. Candlelight is kind to a poor draughtsman: it hides the far corners, and nobody can say what you left out.

The sketch: a small warm room, mostly shadow. The socks came out well. I had not expected to climb a mountain to learn that.

volumes.title: Wind at Rooksgate
volumes.text:
Sketch the ninth. Charcoal, my fingers being too cold for pencil. A thorn tree on the pass at Rooksgate.

Rooksgate is the high gap between two dales, and the wind goes through it like a crowd leaving a hall. There is one thorn tree at the top. It has grown all on one side, leaning out flat, the way a man holds his hat on. I wanted to draw the wind, and you cannot. A signwriter of forty years knows that much: you can only draw what a thing does to its neighbours. So I drew the tree, bent; the grass, combed; and a rook going sideways with great dignity.

The sketch: black and quick, smudged by my sleeve. The book blew shut on it twice and printed a second, fainter tree on the facing page. I have left that one in. It looks like yesterday’s wind.

volumes.title: Four Seconds of Summit
volumes.text:
Sketch the tenth. Pencil. Kettle Crag again, and what I got of it.

I came back to the flat rock under the Crag, where four days ago I waited three hours and drew my boots. The cloud was on the summit as before. I sat. I am Corwen Ashby, I once lettered FERRY in a gale, and I can wait. After an hour my pencil wanted a point. I bent to find my knife in the bottom of the bag. While I was down there a light came over the page, and when I looked up the cloud was closing again, like a curtain when someone has peeped out. Four seconds, perhaps. I saw a notch, and a tilt to the left.

The sketch: one notch, one tilt, and a great deal of blank paper. I laughed out loud, by myself, on a mountain. A rook looked round.

volumes.title: Portrait of a Cloud
volumes.text:
Sketch the eleventh. Charcoal and thumb. The cloud on Kettle Crag.

I have spent two days of my twelve waiting for this summit to come out. This morning it struck me that I was sitting in front of a good subject and asking it to move. The cloud is always there. A man who painted signs for forty years ought to know that you letter the shop that is there, not the one you wish were. So I drew the cloud. It has a shape, once you look: heavy at the west end, torn thin at the east, with a bright rim where the sun leans on it. I rubbed it in with my thumb and lifted the rim out with a crust of bread.

The sketch: a mountain wearing its weather. Nothing in it is ruled, and it is the best page in the book.

volumes.title: A Sign for Stoneladle
volumes.text:
Sketch the twelfth and last. Pencil. The new board at Stoneladle Farm, seen from the road home.

I came down off the Fells last night with eleven sketches and a blister. This morning I asked Mrs. Tolley for the old board that said ST N L DL, and for some paint. I am a signwriter. It took me till dinner. STONELADLE, in a plain capital, and under it, small, Kettle Crag with its cloud on, done freehand with the wrong brush. Marrin, who is eleven and taught me to draw a dog without looking, said the mountain was good. She said the letters were a bit straight. I gave her my second pencil.

The sketch: a gatepost, a board, a lane going down to Emberwick. The board hangs a little low at one end, like their gate. Twelve days ago I would have gone back and levelled it.

volumes.title: Ice in the Wash
volumes.text:
January, Withy Bend. I am Nell Garroway and I keep the ferry here, where the Ember turns for the marsh. I have pulled the Dabchick across on her rope for thirty-four years. This is the year they build the bridge. So I mean to paint the view from the ferry-house window once a month until the bridge is in it and I am out of work.

So far: the far bank, the big willow, the landing stage, a deal of sky. In the water stand six stakes with red rags on, which is all the bridge there is.

I had the window open. I mixed a grey for the sky and it froze. The wash set into ferns and feathers of ice, as on a pane, and dried that way. I could not have painted frost so well on purpose. January did the sky; I did the stakes.

volumes.title: A Brown Month
volumes.text:
February, at the Withy Bend ferry. I paint this window’s view each month, the year they are bridging the Ember, and this month it is brown. The river is brown and in flood to the third step. The willow is a brown fog of twigs. Mr. Strake, the bridge foreman, came over in the Dabchick with a brown dog and looked at his six stakes, of which the river has taken two.

I own five browns and none was right, so I let them run together wet and tipped the board. They made their own river, with a darker thread down the middle where the current goes.

It is all one colour, yet you can tell water from mud from tree. One thing is not brown. Low on the far bank I left a row of specks bare. Snowdrops. They are too small to paint, so I painted round them.

volumes.title: The Wind Takes One
volumes.text:
March. I am the ferrywoman at Withy Bend, painting the same reach of the Ember every month while a bridge is built across it. Today the piles went in. A great iron weight on a frame, hauled up by six men and let drop: thump, and the herons leave; thump, and my cups jump on the dresser.

I took the board outdoors. That was a mistake. I had the sky down, pale, with torn clouds, and the willow just yellowing, when the wind lifted the sheet and laid it face down in the river. It sailed past the landing like a small raft. Mr. Strake’s youngest man fished it out with a boathook.

I did March again indoors with the window shut. The first one hangs on the line beside it. The river has rinsed it to a ghost, every colour gone soft, and it is the better.

volumes.title: Rain Lends a Hand
volumes.text:
April on the Ember, at the Withy Bend ferry, where I paint one picture of the same view each month. Four piers stand in the water now, like teeth coming through. The willow is in leaf, a green so new it is nearly yellow, and the far meadow has lambs on it who run for no reason.

I sat in the doorway under the porch. A shower came across the river sideways and put a dozen drops on my wet sky. Each drop pushed the blue away from itself and left a pale ring with a dark edge. In January I would have fretted. In April I am learning to say thank you.

So there are piers, a willow, lambs as five white gaps, and over them a sky with rain in it. Mr. Strake asked how I had got that effect. I told him I had staff.

volumes.title: Too Many Greens
volumes.text:
May. Nell Garroway, ferrywoman, at the window over Withy Bend, with a bridge half grown outside it. Timber beams lie from pier to pier now. The men walk along them carrying planks, not holding on, whistling. I cannot watch and I cannot look away.

May is all green and I have one green in the box. The willow is a grey green, the meadow a yellow green, the reeds almost blue, and the river reflects the lot and adds brown. I spent the morning mixing on a saucer: blue with this yellow, blue with that, a touch of red to quieten it. Eleven greens by dinner time. The saucer was prettier than most pictures.

This month’s sheet is green on green on green, with one small scarlet dot on the bridge. That is the foreman’s neckerchief. I put it in last, and everything else settled down around it.

volumes.title: Four in the Morning
volumes.text:
June, Withy Bend. I keep the ferry on the Ember, and I am painting this one view each month of the year the bridge is built. In June the light is up before anyone. I was at the window by four, in my coat over my nightgown.

At that hour the river is not a colour at all. It is a strip of sky lying down. Mist stood on it knee high, and out of the mist came the bridge: five piers, the beams, and a handrail along one side only, so that it looked like a comb. The willow hung still.

I used pale pink, pale grey, and bare paper for the mist: the least paint I have ever put on a sheet. At five the first passenger rang the bell on the far bank, and I went down to the Dabchick with pink on my thumb.

volumes.title: Low Water
volumes.text:
July. No rain for five weeks. I am Nell Garroway of the Withy Bend ferry, and my painting of the river this month has very little river in it. The Ember has shrunk to the middle of her bed and left mud flats either side, cracked like an old dish. The Dabchick grounds ten feet short of the stage, and passengers walk the last of it on a plank.

The bridge men, glad of it, work at the piers in dry boots, and the deck is planked a third of the way over.

I have never needed so little water to paint so little water. I dragged a nearly dry brush across the paper and it skipped, leaving sparkle. That is the river. The mud took every brown I own. The rest is heat: a white sky, a tired willow, and two herons standing in the shallows, thinking it over.

volumes.title: The Foreman’s Children
volumes.text:
August at Withy Bend, where I work the ferry and paint the same window’s worth of the Ember each month. The bridge deck reaches two thirds across. Mr. Strake’s children are here, three of them, and they have discovered my table.

I gave them each a corner of paper and a brush. The eldest painted the bridge finished, with a flag. The middle one painted the Dabchick, very large, with me in her, larger. The smallest painted her piece blue and then, gravely, washed the brush in my tea.

My own picture has their marks in it. There is a thumbprint in the meadow that I have made into a cow, and a hard edge in the sky where somebody leaned. Below, a bright gap of water between bridge end and bank, and three small figures on the stage, fishing with string. They caught nothing and reported a good day.

volumes.title: Mist, and the Gap
volumes.text:
September. I am the ferrywoman at Withy Bend. All year I have painted one view from one window, and all year a bridge has crept across it. This morning the last gap was closed. I did not see it done. There was mist on the Ember so thick that the far bank had gone, and the hammering came out of whiteness.

So I painted the mist, which means I painted nearly nothing. I wet the whole sheet and touched in the near landing and the ferry rope going out. Then I let the bridge fade, pier by pier, until the paper was bare.

When it lifted at ten, there the bridge was, bank to bank, and Mr. Strake standing in the middle with his hat off. My picture shows a bridge that sets out and does not arrive. It was true at eight o’clock. I shall let it stand.

volumes.title: Tea for the Willow
volumes.text:
October on the Ember. Nell Garroway, at the ferry-house window, with the tenth of my twelve monthly paintings. The bridge is whole but not open: there is a rope across each end, and the men are tarring the handrails. People still ring the bell for the Dabchick. I pull them over in the shadow of the new bridge and we both look up at it.

The willow has turned. Every leaf is a narrow yellow boat, and they come down and sail off toward the marsh. I ran out of my one orange brown by the second branch. There was cold tea in the pot. I can report that strong tea makes a fair autumn willow, if a pale one, and smells better than paint.

So October is a gold tree, a black tarred rail, and the river carrying a fleet of leaves past the pair of us.

volumes.title: From the Upstairs Window
volumes.text:
November. The Ember is over her banks and into my kitchen, a hand deep, so this month’s painting of Withy Bend is done from the bedroom window with the board on my knees. I have kept the ferry here thirty-four years, and I move the flour upstairs in October as a matter of course.

From up here the view is changed. I can see over the willow. The meadow is a lake with a gate in it. The Dabchick is tied short to the porch and nobody could cross in her. Yet at noon the baker’s cart went over the river, on the bridge, with Mr. Strake walking ahead to lift the rope. Not opened yet; only needed.

I painted grey water to every edge, and one dark firm line across it with a cart on. I see what the thing is for. I mixed that grey quite kindly.

volumes.title: The First to Walk
volumes.text:
December, Withy Bend. Today they opened the bridge, with the town band and a ribbon, and snow lying. I am Nell Garroway. I pulled the ferry here thirty-four years and painted this view every month of my last one. At eleven I took the Dabchick over for the final fare, which was the Mayor, who gave me a shilling and his hand.

Then I walked back across the bridge with my hands in my pockets, the whole way over the Ember. I had never crossed it without a rope in them.

There is hardly any paint in December. The snow is the paper, left alone. Six strokes for the bridge, a grey thread for the willow, one small figure halfway over. The twelve stand along the mantelpiece, stakes to snow. The Dabchick is mine to keep. I mean to fish from her, and to paint the bridge from underneath.

volumes.title: Mrs. Lark at Four
volumes.text:
No. 1. Mrs. Hebe Lark, baker. Oil on board. Taken in payment of one month’s rent.

I am Thea Marchbank, portrait painter. I came to Emberwick on the Monday coach with a commission from the Town Council: one portrait of the Mayor, Mr. Aldous Brimble, in his chain, for the Town Hall stairs. On Tuesday he sent word that he was busy with the drains and would sit next week. I had money for four days. Mrs. Lark, who lets the room over her bakery in Cross Street, said she had always wondered what she looked like to others.

She would only sit while working. So it is four in the morning, and she is to the elbows in dough, with flour on her forearms like white gloves. She is looking at the bread, not at us. She says the nose is hers and the loaves are too small.

volumes.title: The Cobbler’s Best Last
volumes.text:
No. 2. Mr. Osric Tamp, cobbler. Oil on board. Paid for with one pair of boots, resoled.

Still no Mayor. Mr. Brimble, whose portrait I came to Emberwick to paint, is now occupied with the market tolls. Word has gone along Cross Street that the painter over the bakery can be had for goods. Mr. Tamp arrived with an eye on my boots, having noticed them, he said, from behind, on my way to the pump. He wished to be painted in his Sunday collar. I said the apron or nothing. We settled on both, and he holds his best last, a child’s size, worn pale as a bone by sixty years of small shoes.

The picture: a narrow man in a narrow shop, and behind him a wall of boots, every pair waiting for someone. He counted them and said I had left out the vicar’s.

volumes.title: The Lamplighter at Dusk
volumes.text:
No. 3. Miss Petra Vane, lamplighter. Oil on canvas. Paid for with a can of lamp oil and a promise to light my street first.

I am a portrait painter, in Emberwick to paint its Mayor, who this week cannot sit because of a dispute about a hedge. Miss Vane cannot sit either. She has forty-one lamps to light before dark, and she walks eleven miles a day with a pole on her shoulder. I painted her by following her. It took nine evenings and tried Mr. Tamp’s new soles.

It is the corner of Cross Street at dusk, everything blue and going bluer, with one figure reaching up. The only warm colour is the flame at the top of her pole, and the side of her face that it finds. She says it is the first time anyone has looked at her and not at the lamp.

volumes.title: The Constable, Off Duty
volumes.text:
No. 4. Constable Hugo Marl. Oil on board. Paid for with one mended window latch, and a word with the boys who throw things at it.

The Mayor of Emberwick, whom I am here to paint, sends regrets and mentions the Harvest Committee. Constable Marl was on my step at eight. He then stood to attention for three sittings. I have painted statues with more give in them. Each time I asked him to be easy he squared up further, and his chin rose until I could see chiefly neck. On the fourth afternoon my room was warm from the bakery ovens below. He sat down for a moment and went to sleep.

A large man in a small chair, helmet on his knee, collar undone, at peace. I woke him to ask permission. He looked at it a long while and said his mother would like that one.

volumes.title: Mr. Fisk Declines a Face
volumes.text:
No. 5. The hands of Mr. Barnaby Fisk, fishmonger. Oil on board. Paid for with herring, Fridays, until further notice.

Mr. Fisk drives his cart in from the Grey Coast and sells from the market steps. He wanted a portrait for his daughter and did not want his face in it. His face, he said, had frightened better painters than me, and besides, she knew it. So I painted his hands, mending a net across his knees. They are broad, red, scarred white at the knuckles, and they go in and out of the mesh with a needle as neatly as Mrs. Lark plaits a loaf.

I am Thea Marchbank. I came to this town to paint the Mayor, who still cannot sit, and I am beginning not to mind. This one is all hands, net and a brass button. His daughter knew them from across the street.

volumes.title: Class Two, Not Sitting
volumes.text:
No. 6. Class Two of the Ember Lane School, with Miss Adderley. Oil on canvas, the largest I had. Paid for with twenty-three drawings.

First, the Mayor. Mr. Brimble, whose portrait is the reason I am in Emberwick, sat for me on Wednesday for eleven minutes. Then a goat got into the council chamber and he was needed. I have one ear and the start of an eyebrow.

Class Two gave me a whole afternoon and no stillness. Twenty-three children on four benches. I gave up on faces and painted what they were doing: a boy under the bench, two girls sharing one secret, a hand up at the back that had been up for some time. It is a room full of weather. In return each child drew the painter. I have twenty-three portraits of myself, most in a large hat, and I do not own a hat.

volumes.title: Bramble, Who Carries Coal
volumes.text:
No. 7. Bramble, a cart horse, the property of Mr. Dunstan Hale, coal merchant. Oil on canvas. Paid for with two sacks of coal.

I have been half a year in Emberwick waiting to paint its Mayor, and I have learned to take sitters as they come. This one came to the bakery door with the coal and looked in at my window, which is on the first floor. He is seventeen hands. Mr. Hale said if I was painting the town I could not leave out the one who carried it.

Bramble sat, or rather stood, better than the Constable. He moved once in two hours, to eat a geranium. I have him as a grey head in a doorway, with a white blaze shaped like the Grey Coast on the map. One ear is turned back toward Mr. Hale. The geranium is in, as it was before.

volumes.title: What the Bell-Ringer Knew
volumes.text:
No. 8. Mr. Silas Oake, bell-ringer, aged ninety-one. Oil on board. Paid for in information.

Mr. Oake has rung the church bells of Emberwick for seventy-four years and talked for ninety. He sat like a rock and never closed his mouth. I painted it open, as a matter of record: an old man in the belfry window, rope in his fist, mid-sentence, with the roofs of the town behind him.

He knows every face I have done. He knew Mrs. Lark the baker when she could not see over the counter. And he knew the Mayor, whose portrait I was sent here to paint and cannot get, as a boy of nine. A travelling artist drew Aldous Brimble at the fair with ears like jug handles, and pinned it up for the town to laugh at. He has not sat for a likeness since. It was never the drains.

volumes.title: The Postmistress Behind Bars
volumes.text:
No. 9. Mrs. Ines Quarrel, postmistress. Oil on board. Paid for with stamps, and with my letters going first.

I came to Emberwick to paint the Mayor and have painted eight other subjects while he avoids me. I now know why he does, and have written him a note. Mrs. Quarrel took it over the counter, read the envelope on both sides, and told me he would not answer before Michaelmas.

She sat where she always sits, behind the brass grille of the post office. The morning sun comes through it and lays stripes down her face. She would not have them moved. Thirty years, she said, and she would not know herself without them. So: gold bars, a grey bun, spectacles on a chain, and one hand flat on a postcard she has certainly read. She asks me to record that she reads only the fronts.

volumes.title: A Penny a Minute
volumes.text:
No. 10. Pip Lark, aged eight, the baker’s son. Oil, on a board no bigger than a slice of bread. Paid for by the painter, at a penny a minute.

Pip lives downstairs and has watched my sitters come and go. He asked why nobody had asked him. I said boys do not keep still. He said he could, for money. He managed four minutes. In the first he held his breath. In the second he went red. In the third he let it out and was himself, with a gap in his teeth and jam beside it, and I painted like a thief. In the fourth he asked if it was a shilling yet.

One small face, all in a hurry: fourpence. The Mayor, whom I was sent to paint last spring, has answered my note. He says: six in the morning, the allotments, tell no one.

volumes.title: The Mayor Among Beans
volumes.text:
No. 11. Mr. Aldous Brimble, Mayor of Emberwick. Oil on canvas. Paid for by the Town Council, eleven months late.

He was there at six, on the allotments behind the churchyard, in a straw hat, tying up beans. The chain of office hung on a bean pole, out of the soil. I am Thea Marchbank; I have waited since spring to paint this man, and I did not ask him to pose, only to carry on. He talked to the beans, then to me. Somebody drew his ears once and made a joke of them. I said I had no jokes, only paint.

The picture: a stout man in shirtsleeves in a green row, the sun behind him, shining through his ears and turning them shell pink. They are fine ears. He looked for some time. Then he asked if it could hang where people would see it.

volumes.title: Twelve Frames, Town Hall
volumes.text:
No. 12. The Painter, by Class Two, Ember Lane School. Pencil, chalk, and one in gravy. Twenty-three sheets in one frame. Not for sale.

The exhibition opened on Saturday on the Town Hall stairs. The Council had ordered one portrait and has twelve. The Mayor hangs at the top, among his beans. Below him come Bramble the horse, the lamplighter, the sleeping Constable, Mr. Fisk’s hands and the rest, down to Mrs. Lark by the door with her arms in dough. Mr. Oake the bell-ringer explained each, with corrections.

I am Thea Marchbank. I came for four days and it has been a year. I painted eleven of these. The twelfth is the town’s opinion of me: a large hat, in twenty-three versions. Mrs. Lark has offered the room at the old rent, in loaves. On Monday I begin No. 13, the stationmaster. I have bought a hat.

volumes.title: Crow Black
volumes.text:
My name is Dilly Arkwright and I am ten. My Great-Aunt Sabine has given me her paintbox. It is a black tin with a dent in the lid and twelve pans inside, and she painted from it for fifty years. Her hands shake now, so it is mine. Inside the lid is a chart in her writing, with her own name for every colour. Eleven names. The twelfth pan is empty and the chart says: yours.

There is a rule. I may not use a colour until I have found it in Emberwick. One colour each Saturday.

The first is black, and its name is Crow. I thought black would be boring. I sat on the wall by the Corn Exchange and painted the crows on the roof, and when I added water the black went blue at the edges, like their wings. Aunt Sabine said, “There. Now you’ve met.”

volumes.title: The White Called Don’t
volumes.text:
I am Dilly, and I am learning my Great-Aunt Sabine’s paintbox one colour at a time. She gave it to me because her hands shake. Every pan in the box is worn down, some nearly to the tin. Only the white is perfect, smooth as a new soap. On her chart its name is Don’t.

I asked why. She said in watercolour the white is the paper, and anybody who reaches for the white pan has stopped thinking. Then she sent me to find white in Emberwick and paint it without any.

I found the geese on the green. I painted the grass and the pond, and I went round five goose shapes and left them alone. It is hard, not painting something. My tongue stuck out. Aunt Sabine counted. “Five geese, and not a drop of paint in them. Good. Now leave that pan be for fifty years.”

volumes.title: Geranium Red
volumes.text:
Third Saturday with Great-Aunt Sabine’s paintbox, which has twelve pans and a rule: I, Dilly Arkwright, must find each colour in Emberwick before I am allowed to paint with it. Today was the red. On her chart it is called Geranium.

That was easy. Everyone knows where the geraniums are. Mr. Pocock the stationmaster keeps eleven pots along the platform. I sat on the luggage trolley and did all eleven. Red is loud. One brushful, and the whole page turned to look at it.

The trouble came when the red ran into the green leaves and made mud. I showed Aunt Sabine and said sorry. She said mud is only two colours having an argument, and next time I should let one dry before the other speaks. Mr. Pocock wants the picture for the ticket office. I said it has mud in it. He said so has the station.

volumes.title: Butter Yellow
volumes.text:
Fourth Saturday. I am ten, and my Great-Aunt Sabine is teaching me her paintbox by sending me round Emberwick to find its colours. The yellow pan is called Butter, and Saturday is market day, so I knew where to go.

Mrs. Dunn sells butter in Market Square, in pats stamped with a thistle. I asked if I could paint one. She said only if I bought one. So I painted Aunt Sabine’s tea.

Yellow is sneaky. On its own it hardly shows. I put it on three times and it looked like wet paper. Then I painted the shadow under the pat, as blue as I dared, and the butter jumped up. Aunt Sabine had the butter on her toast and the picture on her knee. She said, “Yellow needs a neighbour. Most of us do.” That pan is worn down on one side. She must have liked it.

volumes.title: Duckweed Green
volumes.text:
I am Dilly Arkwright. I have my Great-Aunt Sabine’s paintbox, and I have to find each colour in town before I use it. Saturday five was green. Its name is Duckweed, so I went to the mill pond behind Tanner’s Row, where she lives.

Duckweed is the green skin on the pond that looks solid enough to stand on. It is not. I know because of my left boot. The pan matched it exactly, a flat green, like paint already.

But the pond had other greens that were not in the box: the dark under the alders, the pale new reeds. I mixed in some Butter, then a speck of Crow, and got both. Nobody told me to. Aunt Sabine looked at the picture, then at my boot drying on her fender. She said one green in a tin is plenty for anyone with a yellow and some sense.

volumes.title: Thursday Blue
volumes.text:
Sixth Saturday, and I am halfway through my Great-Aunt Sabine’s paintbox. Six colours found in Emberwick, five to go, and then the twelfth pan, which is empty. Her chart says only: yours. I asked what belongs in it. She said she looked for her twelfth colour for fifty years, all over the county, and never found it. So she left it for me.

Today’s is the light blue. It is called Thursday, after the best sky she ever saw, which was on a Thursday when she was nineteen. The pan is worn to a hole. You can see tin.

I had to find a sky to match, on a Saturday. It rained till four. Then it tore open over the Fells, and I painted it from her back step with my paper on a tray. She held the water jar steady with both hands. That part was hers.

volumes.title: Bridge Stone
volumes.text:
I am Dilly, and I am ten. Every Saturday I take my Great-Aunt Sabine’s paintbox into Emberwick to find one of its colours, and this is the seventh. The colour is a sandy brown. On the chart she calls it Stone.

It is the town bridge. I held the tin up against the wall of it and the pan disappeared. Then I looked round and it was everywhere: the church, the Corn Exchange steps, the front of our own house. The whole town is made of that pan.

I painted the bridge with its three arches and the Ember going under. It took all afternoon, because people kept stopping. An old man said the middle arch was fatter than that. He was right, so I fattened it. Aunt Sabine says Stone is the colour you use most and notice least. There is one in every box, and in most families.

volumes.title: Ember Brown
volumes.text:
Eighth Saturday with the paintbox. It was my Great-Aunt Sabine’s, and I am finding its twelve colours around Emberwick one Saturday at a time. This week it was the dark brown. Its name is Ember, for the river, not for fires.

The Ember had run brown all week. I went down the steps with my jar, and found I had forgotten to bring water. So I dipped the jar in the river.

That is how I found out. The river water was the colour already. I painted the river with the river, hardly touching the pan, and it dried a soft brown with specks in. There is a bit of Emberwick in that picture. Probably a bit of duck. Aunt Sabine laughed until she had to put her tea down. She said she did the same at my age and was cross about it for a week.

volumes.title: Marmalade Orange
volumes.text:
I am Dilly Arkwright, and this is my ninth Saturday finding colours for my Great-Aunt Sabine’s paintbox. She can’t paint because her hands shake, so I go out, and she stays at her window and tells me if I got it right. Today was orange. Her chart calls it Marmalade.

Marmalade is not the jam. Marmalade is the cat at the fishmonger’s. He has been three different cats since Aunt Sabine was young, all orange, all called that.

He sat on a barrel and let me paint him for as long as he wanted. I did him wet, so the edges went furry. For the stripes I waited, then put darker orange on the damp, and they spread just enough. Then he got down, walked across the painting, and left. There are two orange paw prints on it. Aunt Sabine says he has signed it, and it is worth more.

volumes.title: Coast Grey
volumes.text:
Tenth Saturday. My Great-Aunt Sabine gave me her paintbox, and I must find each colour before I use it. The grey could not be found in Emberwick. Its name is Coast. So Dad took me on the branch line to the Grey Coast, with the tin on my knee.

I thought it would be one grey. It was hundreds. The sea was a green grey and the sky a white grey, and the sand a brown grey with the sky lying in it. A gull was the same grey as its rock until it moved.

I painted all of it with one pan and plenty of water. Dad held the paper down with two shoes. On the tideline I found a pebble that matched the pan, and brought it back. Aunt Sabine has one like it on her windowsill, from the summer she bought the tin. Now there are two.

volumes.title: Nearly Night
volumes.text:
Saturday eleven. I am Dilly, and I have found ten of the colours in my Great-Aunt Sabine’s paintbox. The last one with a name is the dark blue. She calls it Nearly Night. She said I would have to stay out late for it, and she had squared it with Mum.

I sat on the churchyard wall at the top of town. First the Fells went blue, then the roofs, then the air. It is not black. It is deeper than that. I painted the sheet with it and lifted out the chimneys with a dry brush.

Then one window lit, down in Tanner’s Row. It was hers. I could see her in the chair, and her old purple cardigan, faded to a soft colour that is not in the tin. I looked in the box. The twelfth pan was empty, and I knew what was going in it.

volumes.title: The Twelfth Pan
volumes.text:
My Great-Aunt Sabine’s paintbox has twelve pans. Eleven had her names on: Crow, Don’t, Geranium, Butter, Duckweed, Thursday, Stone, Ember, Marmalade, Coast, Nearly Night. The twelfth was empty and marked: yours. I am Dilly Arkwright, and on the twelfth Saturday I filled it.

It took all morning. Thursday blue and Geranium red made a purple that shouted. A touch of Stone quietened it. A speck of Coast. Then it was right: a faded heathery colour, gone soft with washing. I poured it into the pan and wrote its name on the chart under hers. Cardigan.

She was asleep in her chair, so I painted her in it. When she woke she looked at the picture, then at her sleeve, and laughed. “Fifty years I hunted that colour all over the county,” she said, “and I was wearing it.” She has asked for the painting. I am keeping the tin.
